Beyond transactions: How PhonePe and Razorpay are using AI to improve digital payments | YourStory Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT PhonePe
India has made digital payments as simple as scanning a QR code. The next opportunity lies in using payments to connect consumers with relevant financial products and help businesses address the challenges of growing online.
At TechSparks 2026, Deep Agrawal, Head of Payments at PhonePe, and Khilan Haria, Chief Product Officer at Razorpay, joined Madanmohan Rao, Research Director at YourStory, for a panel discussion titled ‘Beyond transactions: Solving financial inclusion with contextual money’.
The discussion covered how payments are becoming part of a wider digital experience, from improving transaction success rates to helping merchants attract and retain customers.
Beyond payments: What do users and businesses need?
Agrawal said digital payments have become part of everyday life for more than 500 million UPI users, who use the system to send money to friends, pay electricity bills, shop online, and make payments at stores.
However, the next challenge is to bring another 500 million people into the digital payments ecosystem while helping existing users access financial products beyond payments.
For businesses, accepting payments is only the first step.
Haria said Razorpay’s experience working with millions of small and medium businesses has shown that merchants face several challenges once they have the infrastructure to collect payments, including attracting customers, improving conversions, and encouraging repeat purchases.
“Over the years, we’ve learned as we’ve worked with millions of these SMBs. The larger problem sometimes goes beyond payments. Payments is what I now call the core infrastructure that SMBs need to set up their digital commerce or online business. But beyond that, the struggle most businesses go through is ‘how do I get demand? How do I maximize retention? How do I uplift conversion?’” he said.
Razorpay initially addressed some of these requirements through products for payroll, salary disbursements, and vendor payments.
However, conversations with merchants showed that businesses needed support beyond managing money. They also needed help building and growing their online operations.
Haria said helping more small businesses establish an online presence and succeed in digital commerce could contribute to the growth of India's digital economy.
Using transaction data to improve payments
Every digital transaction generates information that payment platforms can use to better understand customer needs, identify risks and improve the payment experience.
Haria discussed Razorpay's transaction-led foundation model, Vulcan 5.2, which is designed to understand what he described as the language of payments.
According to Haria, each transaction contains nearly 3,000 attributes. By analyzing these, the model can predict missing information, assess the likelihood of fraud, and determine whether a transaction is likely to convert.
This can help businesses identify suspicious transactions, reduce risks, and improve the chances of converting potential buyers into paying customers.
Haria explained that conventional machine learning typically involves identifying patterns, developing hypotheses, and training models around them. Transformer-based models, however, can identify smaller patterns that may be difficult to detect through conventional approaches.
At PhonePe, machine learning is being used to make payments more reliable.
Agrawal discussed an internal model called Kill Switch, which predicts whether a transaction is likely to succeed. It considers factors such as bank response times and recent transaction success rates to assess the likelihood of a successful payment.
“Consumers don't really care whether a transaction fails. What they care about is it should not go into a pending state,” Agrawal said.
“In this model, we tell the customer even before they initiate the transaction that your bank is probably down, come back and do the transaction later.”
Agrawal said this approach helps build trust and encourages users to return to the platform.
Transaction context can also help payment platforms recommend financial products based on customer needs.
For example, a customer booking an international flight through PhonePe may benefit from a travel insurance recommendation. For someone who travels only within India, a bus booking may be more relevant.
Agrawal said PhonePe uses guardrails in its algorithms to avoid recommending products that are not relevant to individual customers.
Razorpay: From AI assistants to autonomous agents
Razorpay is also using AI to help merchants manage everyday business operations.
Haria discussed two initiatives, Ray and Agent Studio, designed to make business support and automation more accessible.
Ray is an AI assistant that functions as an account manager for businesses. While larger customers typically have dedicated account managers, providing similar support to smaller merchants has been difficult to scale.
Ray aims to address this gap by allowing merchants to explain their problems through WhatsApp voice notes or messages in plain English, without navigating complex dashboards and consoles.
Agent Studio goes further by allowing businesses to use autonomous AI agents for specific tasks.
These include recovering abandoned shopping carts, representing merchants in disputes, confirming cash-on-delivery orders and verifying delivery addresses.
Haria said Razorpay had 12 agents live, with 600 brands using them, including some that use multiple agents.
The company plans to increase the number of agents to 100 over the next six months and eventually reach 100,000 businesses using them.
PhonePe: Bringing more users into digital payments
Agrawal also discussed how AI-powered tools could help bring more people into the digital payments ecosystem.
He highlighted the challenges faced by feature-phone users, many of whom live in smaller towns and rural areas or are beginning to participate in the formal economy.
Feature phones have several limitations, including the inability to receive software updates over the air. Users may also need assistance with processes that are familiar to more digitally experienced consumers.
To address these challenges, PhonePe has introduced voice bots that help users with tasks such as linking bank accounts and setting up UPI PINs.
PhonePe is also working to make it easier for micro and small merchants to start selling online.
Building a website using platforms such as Shopify or WooCommerce can be expensive and complicated for young entrepreneurs.
PhonePe's SmartPages product aims to simplify this process by allowing merchants to create a checkout page, list products, and start selling without hiring a web developer or subscribing to a more complex platform.

The IT ministry (MeitY) has proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for training AI models in India.
Called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, the framework aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets to develop AI models while protecting citizens’ privacy and ensuring compliance with the DPDP Act.
The DEPA for AI training also proposes a techno-legal architecture to enable organisations to collaborate on AI model training without directly transferring underlying datasets.
With this, the ministry aims to foster access to datasets for researchers and businesses looking to train AI models. The guidelines have been formulated in collaboration with think tank iSPIRT.
The proposed architecture builds on India’s existing DEPA framework, which already supports consent-based data sharing through initiatives such as Account Aggregator. The new framework encompasses the following technical pillars:
Confidential Clean Rooms: Secure computing environments where organisations can collaborate on data processing and AI model training without exposing the underlying datasets to one another
Differential Privacy: A privacy-preserving technique used to ensure that individual-level information cannot be identified or extracted from an aggregate dataset
Electronic Contracts: Machine-readable agreements that define and enforce data-sharing conditions, including permitted uses, data protection and security requirements
Zero-Trust Security: An approach where every access request is authenticated and authorised, with encryption, continuous monitoring and auditing to protect data
The proposed framework also defines key stakeholders for enabling safe sharing of data for training AI models:
Training Data Providers (TDPs): Organisations that make their data accessible through the framework. For instance: banks, hospitals, government agencies
Training Data Consumers (TDCs): Startups, enterprises, researchers and individuals seeking access to datasets to train AI models
Data Collectives or Data Collabs: Intermediaries that aggregate, standardise, and organise data from various sources and define data-sharing policies and governance rules for participants
Under the DEPA framework, TDPs would first register their datasets on a data exchange platform after anonymising and encrypting them. The datasets would then be tagged with metadata and cryptographic identifiers for traceability.
TDCs can then request a dataset for their specific use cases, and an electronic contract system checks their requests against data-sharing policies and governance rules before granting access.
Once access is given, the model is then trained within a secure data environment using differential privacy methods, ensuring that the raw data remains inaccessible to consumers.
The framework also proposes that trained models must undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling.
Even after deployment, the oversight will continue in the interest of long-term trust and accountability. In line with this, the framework will ensure that TDCs remain subject to continuous monitoring, periodic reviews, and traceability of the model’s outputs back to the data and contracts used in its training.
The launch of the new DEPA framework for AI training comes soon after TRAI also released draft guidelines on the responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. The telecom regulator has sought inputs from stakeholders by November 27.
As per TRAI, its draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines . The centre had earlier released these guidelines to focus on fostering innovation and safe development and deployment of AI offerings, while mitigating risks posed by the technology.
A few weeks ago, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had also said that the centre will release a consultation paper for regulation on AI safety and security within a month. Earlier reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation .

[83] YourStory — Waiting for an AI law is a poor compliance strategy
URL: https://yourstory.com/2026/10/waiting-for-an-ai-law-is-a-poor-compliance-strategy
Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT Waiting for an AI law is a poor compliance strategy | YourStory A bank has an AI system in place to flag suspicious transactions and take the call to freeze accounts. While the workflow has a human sign-off in place, clearing around 400 cases a day has resulted in the approval system becoming a formality. So, when a wrongly-frozen account takes the system to court, the bank becomes unable to prove what the human actually reviewed. This, unfortunately, is no longer a hypothetical scenario.
On July 2, 2026, the Supreme Court of India quashed orders passed by the National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal in the Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd. case . The orders had rested on citations generated by an AI tool and attributed to the Supreme Court itself. This directed the Bar Council of India to constitute a committee to prescribe disciplinary norms for advocates who file AI-generated citations.
This is a business story as much as a legal one. Despite two tribunals and several rounds of proceedings, the parties had to carry the cost of a machine error that no human caught before filing. No AI statute was required to reach that outcome. Ordinary law, applied by judges, did the work.
The regulators are moving faster than the legislature
For most Indian companies, the sharper edge is coming from sectoral regulators rather than from the bench.
In early June this year, the Reserve Bank of India gave banks and other regulated entities until June 30 to submit gap assessments on frontier-AI cyber risk. Instead of having the CISO to file the note, the RBI had asked the board to sign one.
Later, on June 24, the RBI publicly released a draft 'Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management' to establish a comprehensive enterprise-wide model governance framework for the financial sector. Here 'models' extend to third-party models, AI, and machine learning (ML) systems used by commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, NBFCs, and other financial institutions. So if a lending decision is influenced by a model licensed from a vendor, the model risk sits on the one putting the AI system to use and not the vendor who built it.
Meanwhile, India's legislative position is still a work-in-progress. On October 8, 2026, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had assured that the time has come for India to get an AI law. In a first step towards this, the government will be launching a consultation paper on regulating artificial intelligence.
However, any business that is treating a pending law as its compliance milestone has their sequencing backwards. Even when the statute arrives, it can only land on top of existing case laws and sectoral circulars, not in place of them. Regardless of what law comes into place, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act takes full effect on May 13, 2027. Businesses will be held accountable even if the data is being processed by an external vendor as the DPDPA will be applicable wherever an AI system handles personal data.
Behind all the legal vocabulary, the requirements across all the domains are the same—one needs to show their working.
For any consequential decision made by an AI system, organisations must be able to have the visibility regarding which model produced the output, what data it drew on, whether a retrieval step was involved, who reviewed it before it went out, and whether that record still exists six months later.
Multiple Indian firms have written a policy, appointed a committee, and deployed systems but can still not answer any of the above questions. This is clearly an architecture question before it is a policy-related one. Recording the model version, prompt, retrieved data and human sign-off for every AI decision is only cheap if it is thoughtfully designed for. It can, however, become close to impossible to reconstruct afterwards.
It is important for businesses to question an AI vendor before procuring a model. Does the system record which model version handled each request? Can that record be exported and retained? Where does inference physically happen? What happens to inputs after processing? Where in the workflow is a human required to act? Vendors that cannot answer plainly are transferring risk to the buyer.
There is not much point in waiting for an AI law. AI adoption is already in full swing, and when unprepared, the chain is only waiting to break. In the case of the tribunal matter, that chain broke at the review step. In an RBI-regulated entity, the chain is most likely to break earlier, at provenance, if nobody logged which version of which model scored the application.
The current strategy, albeit unglamorous, is to ensure that the record of every AI-assisted decision made can survive being read aloud. So while the law may still be pending, the question is not. When it does come, the answer will have to exist already.
(The article has been authored by Ramprakash Ramamoorthy, Director - AI Research, Zoho Corporation)

Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math , Altman said:
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro , the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

Measuring AI progress on the tasks that matter in everyday life.
Share OpenAI’s mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. For the more than one billion people who currently use ChatGPT every week, we want to build AI that can help with the practical challenges of everyday life, like finding childcare, accessing government services, creating a budget, preparing for school, modifying recipes, ordering groceries, designing workout plans, and more.
When someone is looking for help making their life easier, they need more than advice or a chat response. To be a truly helpful personal assistant, ChatGPT should be able to take actions that actually get things done.
To measure model performance over time on everyday tasks, we built an evaluation of tasks covering areas where users wanted the most help from AI and personal agents. We used this evaluation to track and drive improvement in model performance on everyday tasks over the past year.
To identify the tasks people value most, we started with two large studies that track how people spend time in both the U.S. and internationally: the American Time Use Survey ⁠ (opens in a new window) and the Multinational Time Use Study ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Together, these datasets provide a detailed catalog of everyday life tasks that people do across different demographics, times of day, and seasons. To understand where people would most value AI assistance, we expanded on these existing surveys with a new demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents. For each task, we asked a variety of questions to identify the areas where everyday people most wanted help from a personal assistant. The resulting tasks span the most important areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services.
Below are some examples of how our current models perform on practical workflows from everyday life.
Enroll in the right kindergarten after moving

Our latest models score very highly on many LifeVal tasks. See more
Over the past year, we’ve trained our models to become much faster, more capable, and more aligned on browser use, computer use, and connectors tasks. Enabling these capabilities in ChatGPT also expands the types of tasks the model can help with, helping move ChatGPT beyond a chat tool and towards a truly agentic personal assistant.
To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we need to measure and improve model progress on what matters in the lives of everyday people. That means going beyond academic assessments of model knowledge and actually measuring how well AI models can help people navigate decisions, manage everyday responsibilities, and get meaningful things done. We are hopeful that LifeVal represents a step towards that goal.

Grok has a very specific edge over other AI models: live access to X, so your agents can keep their finger on the pulse a little more easily. But outside of that, Grok models and agents are still solid alternatives to what OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have on offer. And if you're using Grok for work, you'll want to connect it to the rest of your tech stack. The most secure and easiest way to do that is with Zapier.
There are two main ways to automate Grok with Zapier. You can add Grok to the workflows you already run in Zapier, so it does research, analyzes inputs, or makes images whenever something happens in your other apps. Or you can install Zapier inside Grok Bot or Grok Build and ask your AI assistant to act across 9,000+ apps without leaving the chat.
Build automations from wherever you work. Describe the outcome you want, and Zapier connects your tools, runs the steps, and stays on the job after you close the chat. Combine AI with reliable, deterministic automation across 9,000+ apps. Get started for free.

Zapier is built for workflows that need to run the same way every time, but some of them benefit from reasoning somewhere along the line. Zapier's Grok integration lets you drop a Grok step into any Zap, right where it's useful.
You don't want an AI model running every step—that's a recipe for token burn . Moving a form submission into your CRM, for example, doesn't need reasoning, so it's a job for deterministic automation. Researching the company behind that submission, drafting an outline from a one-line brief, or spotting what's trending on social media, on the other hand, are the kinds of tasks where Grok shines.
Here's an example. Say a new lead lands in Salesforce. A Zap picks it up, sends the company name to Grok with a prompt like "Find recent news and industry challenges for this company and summarize them in three sentences," then writes the summary back to the lead record so your rep sees it before the first call. Grok only runs when there's a new lead to research, and everything around it behaves the same way each time.
Beyond asking Grok, you can also do things like categorizing text, extracting data, and generating images.
You connect your own SpaceXSI account with an API key, so Grok usage is billed by SpaceXSI on top of the Zapier tasks your Zap uses. If you'd rather use a model that's built into Zapier, with no separate account or token billing, check out which models are available through AI by Zapier .
Here are a few ways you might bring Grok into your Zapier workflows:
Enrich new leads. When a lead is added to your CRM or submitted through a form, have Grok research the company and log recent announcements and industry challenges. Try the Salesforce version .
Turn briefs into outlines or first drafts. When a new record lands in Airtable, Asana, or Notion, send the brief to Grok and have the outline land in a Google Doc, a Notion page, or your team's Slack channel for review.
Track trending topics. Schedule a Zap to ask Grok what's trending on a topic you care about every hour, day, or week, then send the results to Slack, Gmail, or a spreadsheet you can mine for content ideas. Try the daily Slack version .
Generate images from a spreadsheet. Write prompts in Trello cards, Airtable records, or Google Sheets rows, and have Grok create the image and attach it right back to where the prompt came from. This can be handy for webinar slides and social posts when a stock photo won't cut it.
